questions.assertion: For the same net force, a lighter object gets a larger acceleration than a heavier one.
questions.reason: One newton is defined as the force that produces an acceleration of 1 m s⁻² on an object of mass 1 kg.
questions.answer: b
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but R is not the explanation of A. A follows from Newton's second law, a = F/m, in which the acceleration is inversely proportional to the mass. R only defines the unit of force; it does not say how acceleration depends on mass.

questions.assertion: A fielder pulls their hands backwards along with the ball just after catching a fast-moving cricket ball.
questions.reason: Increasing the time in which the velocity of the ball falls to zero increases the force the fielder must apply.
questions.answer: c
questions.explanation: A is true. R is false — it states the opposite of what happens. Pulling the hands back increases the time over which the velocity falls to zero, which reduces the magnitude of the acceleration and therefore, by F = ma, reduces the force needed. That is exactly why the fielder does it, and why the catch hurts less.

questions.stem: State Newton's first law of motion. Use it to explain why passengers standing in a bus lean backwards when the bus suddenly starts moving.
questions.answer: Newton's first law of motion: an object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues to move with a constant velocity, unless a net force acts upon the object. When the bus suddenly starts, the floor of the bus and the passengers' feet are carried forward by the bus, but the upper part of each passenger's body is not acted upon by any net force in the forward direction and so tends to stay where it was, at rest. The body therefore appears to lean backwards. This tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of rest or of uniform motion is called inertia.
valuePoints: States the first law correctly, including that a net force is needed to change the state of rest or of constant velocity
The feet move forward with the bus while the upper body tends to remain at rest, so the passenger leans backwards
Names the tendency as inertia

rubric.label: Statement of the law
rubric.descriptor: Rest stays rest and motion stays uniform unless a net force acts

rubric.label: Application to the bus
rubric.descriptor: Upper body tends to stay at rest while the feet are carried forward; mentions inertia

questions.stem: A block lies on a table. In case (i) two forces of 10 N and 6 N both act on it towards the right. In case (ii) a force of 10 N acts towards the right and a force of 6 N towards the left. Find the magnitude and the direction of the net force in each case.
questions.answer: (i) The two forces are in the same direction, so the magnitude of the net force is their sum: 10 N + 6 N = 16 N, acting towards the right. (ii) The two forces are opposite in direction and unequal in magnitude, so the magnitude of the net force is the difference between them: 10 N − 6 N = 4 N, acting towards the right, that is along the direction of the larger force.
valuePoints: Same direction: net force = 10 + 6 = 16 N towards the right
Opposite directions: net force = 10 − 6 = 4 N, in the direction of the larger force, that is towards the right

rubric.label: Case (i)
rubric.descriptor: 16 N towards the right, with the reason that forces in the same direction add

rubric.label: Case (ii)
rubric.descriptor: 4 N towards the right, along the larger force

questions.stem: A weightlifter holds a barbell steady above her head. The bar has a mass of 10 kg and a mass of 10 kg is fixed at each end of it. How much force is she applying, and in which direction? Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
questions.answer: Total mass of the barbell = 10 kg + 10 kg + 10 kg = 30 kg. The gravitational force with which the Earth pulls it downwards is F = mg = 30 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² = 294 N. The barbell is held steady, so it is not accelerating and the forces on it must be balanced. The weightlifter therefore applies an equal force of 294 N in the upward direction.
valuePoints: Total mass = 30 kg
F = mg = 30 × 9.8 = 294 N downwards, so she applies 294 N upwards to balance it

rubric.label: Weight of the barbell
rubric.descriptor: Total mass 30 kg and F = mg = 294 N

rubric.label: Force applied
rubric.descriptor: 294 N upwards, with the reason that the forces must balance for it to stay steady

questions.stem: A student tries to push a stationary block of mass 25 kg along a horizontal floor. The maximum force of friction opposing the motion is 50 N. Find the displacement of the block in 2 s if the student pushes with a constant force of (i) 50 N and (ii) 55 N in the forward direction.
questions.answer: (i) The force applied is exactly equal to the opposing force of friction, so the two forces are balanced and the net force on the block is zero. By Newton's first law the block, which was at rest, stays at rest: its displacement in 2 s is 0 m. (ii) Net force = 55 N − 50 N = 5 N in the forward direction. By Newton's second law, a = F/m = 5 N / 25 kg = 0.2 m s⁻² in the forward direction. The block starts from rest, so u = 0, and s = ut + ½at² = 0 × 2 + ½ × 0.2 × 2² = ½ × 0.2 × 4 = 0.4 m. The displacement is 0.4 m in the forward direction.
valuePoints: With 50 N the forces are balanced, the net force is zero and the block does not move: displacement 0 m
With 55 N the net force is 5 N, so a = 5/25 = 0.2 m s⁻²

rubric.label: Case (i)
rubric.descriptor: Net force zero, block stays at rest, displacement 0 m

rubric.label: Acceleration in case (ii)
rubric.descriptor: Net force 5 N and a = 0.2 m s⁻² from F = ma

rubric.label: Displacement in case (ii)
rubric.descriptor: 0.4 m using s = ut + ½at² with u = 0

questions.stem: Calculate the gravitational force with which the Earth pulls (i) a sack of mass 12 kg and (ii) a stone of mass 0.5 kg, taking g = 9.8 m s⁻². (iii) The sack is much heavier than the stone. Does the Earth give them different accelerations when they fall freely? Give a reason.
questions.answer: (i) F = mg = 12 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² = 117.6 N, directed downwards, towards the Earth. (ii) F = mg = 0.5 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² = 4.9 N, also directed downwards. (iii) No. Although the force on the sack is much larger, its mass is larger in exactly the same proportion, and the acceleration is a = F/m = mg/m = g for both. The acceleration due to the gravitational force by the Earth does not depend on the mass of the object, so near the Earth's surface both fall with the same acceleration of 9.8 m s⁻².
valuePoints: F = mg = 12 × 9.8 = 117.6 N downwards
F = mg = 0.5 × 9.8 = 4.9 N downwards
a = F/m = mg/m = g, so the acceleration is the same for both and does not depend on mass

rubric.label: Force on the sack
rubric.descriptor: 117.6 N, with the direction downwards

rubric.label: Same acceleration
rubric.descriptor: States a = g for both and shows that the mass cancels in a = mg/m

questions.stem: Explain each of the following in terms of the time taken for the velocity to change and the force that results: (i) an airbag inflates in a vehicle during a collision, (ii) a landing mat or sand bed is placed for a high jumper, (iii) a coconut brought down hard on a stone floor cracks open.
questions.answer: (i) In a collision the vehicle comes to an abrupt halt. The airbag inflates quickly into a soft, compressible cushion, so the passenger's head and chest push into the bag instead of striking the hard steering wheel or dashboard. The time over which the passenger's velocity falls to zero is increased, which reduces the acceleration and, by F = ma, the force acting on the person, thereby lowering the risk of serious injury. (ii) The landing mat or sand bed works the same way: it compresses as the athlete lands, so their velocity falls to zero over a longer time. The acceleration, and hence the force on the athlete, is smaller than it would be on hard ground. (iii) Here the effect is used the other way round. The coconut hits a hard surface at high velocity and stops in a very short time, so the change in its velocity is extremely rapid. To produce so large an acceleration the ground must exert a very large force on it, and it is this large force that breaks the shell.
valuePoints: Airbag: increases the time in which the passenger stops, so acceleration and hence force are reduced
Landing mat: the same reasoning applied to the athlete's landing
Coconut: it stops in a very short time, so the acceleration and hence the force from the ground are very large, cracking the shell

rubric.label: Airbag
rubric.descriptor: Longer stopping time gives smaller acceleration and therefore smaller force

rubric.label: Landing mat
rubric.descriptor: Same explanation applied to the high jumper

rubric.label: Coconut
rubric.descriptor: Very short stopping time gives a very large force, which breaks the shell

questions.stem: A sports car of mass 1500 kg is moving towards the east along a straight road. Its velocity-time graph consists of three straight portions: from 0 s to 5 s the velocity rises uniformly from 0 to 10 m s⁻¹; from 5 s to 10 s it stays at 10 m s⁻¹; from 10 s to 15 s it falls uniformly from 10 m s⁻¹ to 0. Calculate the force acting on the car during each of the three intervals, stating its direction, and explain what the sign of your answer means.
questions.answer: 0 s to 5 s: the graph is a straight line inclined to the time axis, so the acceleration is constant. Using v = u + at with u = 0, v = 10 m s⁻¹ and t = 5 s, we get 10 = 0 + a × 5, so a = 2 m s⁻². By Newton's second law, F = ma = 1500 kg × 2 m s⁻² = 3000 N acting towards the east, that is in the direction of motion. 5 s to 10 s: the graph is parallel to the time axis, so the velocity is constant and the acceleration is zero. Therefore F = ma = 1500 × 0 = 0 N; no net force acts on the car. 10 s to 15 s: using v = u + at with u = 10 m s⁻¹, v = 0 and t = 5 s, we get 0 = 10 + a × 5, so a = −2 m s⁻². Then F = 1500 × (−2) = −3000 N. The negative sign means that this force acts in the direction opposite to the direction of motion, that is towards the west; it is the braking force, which is why the car slows down. Note that the car is moving fastest during the middle interval and yet no net force acts on it: a force is needed not to keep an object moving but to change its velocity.
valuePoints: 0 to 5 s: a = 2 m s⁻² and F = 1500 × 2 = 3000 N towards the east
5 to 10 s: constant velocity, a = 0, so the net force is zero
10 to 15 s: a = −2 m s⁻² and F = −3000 N, that is 3000 N towards the west
The negative sign means the force is opposite to the direction of motion
A high constant velocity needs no net force; force is needed only to change velocity

rubric.label: First interval
rubric.descriptor: a = 2 m s⁻² (half) and F = 3000 N east (1)

rubric.label: Second interval
rubric.descriptor: Zero acceleration and zero net force, with the reason from the shape of the graph

rubric.label: Third interval
rubric.descriptor: a = −2 m s⁻² (half) and F = 3000 N towards the west (1)

rubric.label: Meaning of the sign
rubric.descriptor: Force opposite to the direction of motion; a constant velocity needs no net force

questions.stem: For a long time it was believed that a force is needed to keep an object moving at a constant velocity. Explain why everyday experience suggests this, describe the thought experiment in which the force of friction between an object and a horizontal floor is zero, and state what Newton's first law says instead. Then explain, using this law, (i) why you must keep pedalling a bicycle on a level road and (ii) why a person pushing a box at constant velocity is applying a force even though the net force is zero.
questions.answer: Everyday experience suggests that a force is needed because every moving object around us slows down and stops when we stop pushing it: a ball rolls to a halt, a bicycle stops if you stop pedalling. What is easy to miss is that the force of friction is always present between the surfaces in contact, acting opposite to the direction of motion, and it is this force that brings the object to rest. In the thought experiment we imagine an object and a horizontal floor so smooth that the force of friction between them is zero. If such an object were given a push and then released, nothing would act on it along the direction of its motion, its velocity would not decrease at all, and it would continue moving forever without ever coming to rest. Galileo argued in this way that if all impediments to the motion of a body along a horizontal plane are removed, it will continue to move indefinitely. Newton's first law of motion states this as: an object at rest remains at rest, and an object in motion continues to move with a constant velocity, unless a net force acts upon the object. In other words, if the net force is zero, the acceleration is zero. (i) On a level road, friction between the tyres and the road, and the friction of the air, act against the bicycle's motion. You must keep pedalling to apply a forward force that cancels these, so that the net force is zero and the velocity stays constant; if you stop, friction is the only force left, the net force is no longer zero, and the bicycle slows down. (ii) A person pushing a box at constant velocity is applying a force equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force of friction on the box. The two forces balance, so the net force on the box is zero and by the first law the box keeps moving at constant velocity. The person's force is real and necessary, but its whole task is to cancel friction, not to maintain the motion.
valuePoints: Everyday objects stop because friction acts opposite to the motion, which hides the real rule
Thought experiment: with zero friction a moving object would never slow down and would keep moving forever
Newton's first law: rest stays rest and motion stays uniform unless a net force acts; zero net force means zero acceleration
Bicycle: pedalling supplies a forward force that cancels friction, keeping the net force zero
Pushing a box: the applied force balances friction, so the net force is zero and the velocity is constant

rubric.descriptor: Friction is always present and acts opposite to the motion, bringing objects to rest

rubric.label: Thought experiment
rubric.descriptor: With zero friction the object's velocity would not decrease and it would move on indefinitely

rubric.label: Statement of the first law
rubric.descriptor: Correct statement, including the condition of no net force

rubric.label: The bicycle
rubric.descriptor: Pedalling cancels friction so the net force is zero; stopping leaves friction as the only force

rubric.label: The box
rubric.descriptor: Applied force balances friction; net force zero, so constant velocity continues

questions.passage: Four coins are stacked and taped together. A rubber band is held slightly stretched between the finger and thumb, with two marks A and B at its ends and a third mark C showing how far it will be pulled back. The stack of coins is pushed back against the band until it reaches C and is then released, and the distance the stack travels before coming to rest is measured. The whole procedure is repeated on three different level surfaces, stretching the band to C every time. The distances measured are: wooden table top 38 cm, laminated table top 61 cm, polished marble floor 96 cm. A spring balance is then used on each surface: a wooden block is attached to its hook and pulled with a gradually increasing force, and the reading is noted at the moment the block just begins to move. The readings are 2.6 N on the wooden top, 1.7 N on the laminated top and 1.1 N on the marble floor.

parts.prompt: Which surface has the smallest force of friction acting between it and the object moving on it?

options.text: the wooden table top
the laminated table top
the polished marble floor
the three surfaces cannot be compared from these readings

parts.answer: (c) — the marble floor gives both the largest distance travelled by the stack of coins (96 cm) and the smallest spring balance reading (1.1 N). Both observations point the same way: less friction, so the velocity of the stack decreases more slowly and it travels further.

parts.prompt: Why must the rubber band be stretched to the same mark C on every surface?
parts.answer: So that the same force, and therefore the same initial velocity, is given to the stack of coins each time. Only then can any difference in the distance travelled be attributed to the surface, which is the one thing being changed.

parts.prompt: After the stack of coins loses contact with the rubber band it slows down and stops. Name the forces acting on it before and after it leaves the band, and explain what the spring balance reading measures.
parts.answer: While in contact with the band, the forward force of the stretched rubber band and the backward force of friction both act on the stack. The band's force is the larger, so a net force acts forward and the stack accelerates from rest. Once it loses contact, the band's force is gone and only the force of friction acts, opposite to the direction of motion; it gradually decreases the velocity and finally brings the stack to rest (1 mark). The spring balance reading taken at the instant the block just begins to move is an approximate measure of the force of friction between the block and that surface, because up to that instant the applied force and friction are balanced; a smaller reading means a smaller force of friction (1 mark).

questions.assertion: A girl carrying a box on her head and walking on level ground does no work on the box by the upward force she applies to it.
questions.reason: The upward force she applies is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement of the box.
questions.answer: a
questions.explanation: Both are true and R explains A: work done by a force is the force multiplied by the displacement in the direction of the force. Here the box has no displacement in the direction of her upward force, so the work done by that force is zero — even though she feels tired.

questions.assertion: If the magnitude of the velocity of a vehicle is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes four times as large.
questions.reason: The kinetic energy of an object is directly proportional to its mass.
questions.answer: b
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but R is not the explanation of A. A follows from the dependence of kinetic energy on the square of the velocity in K = ½mv², so doubling v makes K four times as large. R describes the dependence on mass, which is not involved here since the mass is unchanged.

questions.stem: While saving a goal, a goalkeeper's hands move back by 15 cm as she stops the ball, applying a force of 200 N. How much work does she do on the ball? Explain the sign of your answer.
questions.answer: The goalkeeper applies a force in the direction opposite to the motion of the ball, so the displacement of the ball must be taken as negative with respect to the direction of the force: s = −0.15 m. Work done on the ball = force × displacement in the direction of the force = 200 N × (−0.15 m) = −30 J. The negative sign means that the work done by the goalkeeper on the ball is negative, because the displacement of the ball is opposite to the direction of the force she applies; this is why the ball loses energy and stops.

questions.stem: A weightlifter lifts a 75 kg mass through a height of 2 m in 5 s. Find the work she does and the power required. Take g = 10 m s⁻².
questions.answer: Work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force. To lift the mass slowly she must apply an upward force equal to mg, so W = mgh = 75 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 2 m = 1500 J. Power is the rate at which work is done: P = W/t = 1500 J / 5 s = 300 W.

questions.stem: A cricket ball of mass 0.2 kg is bowled at a velocity of 43 m s⁻¹. Calculate its kinetic energy at the moment of delivery.
questions.answer: Kinetic energy K = ½mv² = ½ × 0.2 kg × (43 m s⁻¹)² = ½ × 0.2 × 1849 = 184.9 J. The kinetic energy of the ball is 184.9 J.

questions.stem: A stone of mass 2 kg is held at the top of a building 20 m high and then allowed to fall freely. Taking g = 10 m s⁻² and neglecting air resistance, find (i) its potential energy at the top, (ii) its kinetic energy just before it reaches the ground and (iii) its velocity just before it reaches the ground.
questions.answer: (i) Potential energy at the top, U = mgh = 2 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 20 m = 400 J. (ii) At the top the stone is at rest, so its kinetic energy is zero and its mechanical energy is 400 J. As it falls, its potential energy decreases and its kinetic energy increases by the same amount, the mechanical energy staying constant because only the gravitational force acts. Just before it reaches the ground its height is zero, so its potential energy is zero and all 400 J has become kinetic energy: K = 400 J. (iii) K = ½mv², so 400 = ½ × 2 × v², which gives v² = 400 and v = 20 m s⁻¹, directed downwards.

400 = ½ × 2 × v² gives v = 20 m s⁻¹

questions.stem: A person uses a straight ramp to raise a load over a step 30 cm high. The foot of the ramp is 40 cm away from the step, so the sloping surface of the ramp is 50 cm long. Calculate the mechanical advantage of the ramp, and explain why using it does not reduce the total work the person must do.
questions.answer: For an inclined plane, mechanical advantage = load / effort = L / h, where L is the length of the sloping surface and h is the height raised. Here L = 50 cm and h = 30 cm, so mechanical advantage = 50/30 = 1.67 (to two decimal places). The effort needed is therefore about 1.67 times smaller than the load. Using the ramp does not reduce the total work, because work is the product of force and displacement. The force is smaller, but the load must be pushed through 50 cm along the ramp instead of being lifted through 30 cm, and the extra distance exactly makes up for the smaller force. A simple machine changes the magnitude or the direction of the force that must be applied; it makes the task easier, but it does not create energy and does not reduce the work to be done.
valuePoints: Mechanical advantage of an inclined plane = L/h
Work is unchanged: the smaller force acts through a larger distance, and a machine does not create energy

questions.stem: A child slides down a smooth slide whose top is 3.2 m above the ground. Taking g = 10 m s⁻² and neglecting friction, find the magnitude of the child's velocity on reaching the bottom. Would a heavier child, or a slide of a different shape but the same height, change your answer? Give a reason.
questions.answer: At the top the child has potential energy mgh and no kinetic energy; at the bottom the height is zero, so all of it has become kinetic energy ½mv². Neglecting friction, mechanical energy is conserved, so ½mv² = mgh. The mass m cancels from both sides, giving v² = 2gh and v = the square root of (2gh) = the square root of (2 × 10 × 3.2) = the square root of 64 = 8 m s⁻¹. Neither a heavier child nor a differently shaped slide would change this answer. The mass cancels out of the equation, so it does not appear in the result; and the velocity depends only on the height h through which the child descends, not on the path taken to get down. A longer or more curved slide of the same height gives the same speed at the bottom (though in practice friction would reduce it).

questions.stem: A coconut of mass 1.5 kg falls from the top of a coconut tree 10 m tall onto wet sand on a beach, and comes to rest by making a depression in the sand. Take g = 10 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance. (i) Calculate its potential energy at the top of the tree. (ii) Calculate the magnitude of its velocity just before it hits the sand. (iii) If the average resistive force of the sand is 3000 N and all the coconut's energy is used in making the depression, calculate the depth of the depression. (iv) State what happens to the energy of the coconut in the end.
questions.answer: (i) Potential energy at the top, U = mgh = 1.5 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 10 m = 150 J. (ii) Mechanical energy is conserved during the fall, so just before impact all of this has become kinetic energy: ½mv² = 150 J, giving ½ × 1.5 × v² = 150, so v² = 200 and v = the square root of 200, about 14.1 m s⁻¹, directed downwards. (iii) Inside the sand the coconut is brought to rest, so its kinetic energy of 150 J must be reduced to zero. The sand applies a resistive force of 3000 N opposite to the motion, and the work done by this force over a depth d is 3000 N × d, taken as negative because the force opposes the displacement. Using the work-energy theorem, the magnitude of the work done by the sand equals the kinetic energy lost: 3000 N × d = 150 J, so d = 150/3000 = 0.05 m, that is 5 cm. (iv) The energy has not disappeared. Work done against the resistance of the sand pushes the grains apart and makes the depression; the rest of the energy appears as heat and sound in the sand and in the coconut. Energy has been transferred and changed in form, not destroyed.

Work done against the sand = 3000 × d, and by the work-energy theorem this equals 150 J
The energy is used in displacing the sand and appears as heat and sound; it is not destroyed

questions.stem: Simple machines make a task easier without reducing the work to be done. (i) Explain what a fixed pulley does for us and state its mechanical advantage, with a reason. (ii) Name the three parts of a lever and write the relation between effort, effort arm, load and load arm. (iii) A seesaw has a fulcrum at C and four seats: A and E at 2 m from C on opposite sides, and B and D at 1 m from C on opposite sides. A child of mass 15 kg sits at seat A. On which seat should a child of mass 30 kg sit so that the seesaw is balanced? Show your working.
questions.answer: (i) A fixed pulley is a wheel with a groove that guides a rope, fixed at the top. It does not reduce the magnitude of the force required; it only changes the direction in which the force must be applied, so that a load can be raised by pulling downwards on the rope instead of lifting upwards, which is far more convenient. Since the effort and the load are equal in magnitude, the mechanical advantage of a fixed pulley = load/effort = 1. (ii) The three parts of a lever are the fulcrum, the fixed point about which the lever rotates; the load, the force to be overcome; and the effort, the force applied. The distance of the load from the fulcrum is the load arm and the distance of the effort from the fulcrum is the effort arm. A lever balances when effort × effort arm = load × load arm, and its mechanical advantage = load/effort = effort arm / load arm. (iii) The seesaw is a lever with its fulcrum at C. Let the 30 kg child sit at a distance L from the fulcrum, on the side opposite to A. For balance, 15 kg × 2 m = 30 kg × L, so 30 = 30 × L and L = 1 m. A seat 1 m from the fulcrum, on the side opposite A, is seat D. The heavier child must sit nearer the fulcrum, on the shorter arm: the smaller force needs the longer arm.
valuePoints: A fixed pulley changes only the direction of the effort, not its magnitude
Mechanical advantage of a fixed pulley = 1, since load and effort are equal
Lever: fulcrum, load and effort; effort × effort arm = load × load arm
15 × 2 = 30 × L gives L = 1 m
The 30 kg child should sit at seat D, nearer the fulcrum, on the opposite side

questions.passage: For a school science exhibition, two friends measure their own power on the staircase of their school block. The staircase rises through a vertical height of 4 m from the ground floor to the first floor. Rahul, whose mass is 50 kg, walks up steadily and a classmate times him at 8 s. Anjali, whose mass is 40 kg, runs up the same staircase and is timed at 5 s. The friends take the acceleration due to the gravitational force by the Earth as 10 m s⁻² and ignore any energy used in moving their arms and legs sideways. They then argue about who has done more work and who is more powerful.

parts.prompt: The work done by each of them against the gravitational force in climbing the staircase depends on

options.text: their mass and the time they took
their mass and the vertical height climbed
the number of steps and the time they took
the length of the sloping staircase alone

parts.answer: (b) — the work done against gravity is mgh, so it depends on the mass and on the vertical height gained, and not on how long it took or on the path followed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the work done by Rahul in climbing the staircase.
parts.answer: Work done = mgh = 50 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 4 m = 2000 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the power developed by each friend, and use your answers to settle their argument.
parts.answer: Rahul: W = mgh = 50 × 10 × 4 = 2000 J, so P = W/t = 2000 J / 8 s = 250 W. Anjali: W = mgh = 40 × 10 × 4 = 1600 J, so P = 1600 J / 5 s = 320 W (1 mark for both calculations). Rahul does more work, 2000 J against Anjali's 1600 J, because he is heavier and raises a greater mass through the same height. Anjali is nevertheless more powerful, 320 W against 250 W, because power is the rate at which work is done and she did her work in a shorter time. Both are right about different quantities: doing more work and being more powerful are not the same thing (1 mark).
